meta.title: It's OK to use coding assistance tools to revive the projects you never were going to finish
meta.author: inactive-user

comments.author: confusedcyborg
comments.text: It's also okay to accumulate projects you are going to someday(tm) finish.

comments.author: downrightnifty
comments.text: The title seems inconsistent with the article; whether or not it's "okay" (whatever that means) isn't really addressed aside from a small section at the end that doesn't consider any ethical factors, consisting only of the author reassuring theirself that they won't lose their own programming skills by making use of AI in this way (nothing on how their use of AI might affect anyone else). You could just as easily argue that it's not okay despite the results that were demonstrated.

comments.author: tonyg
comments.text: Is it? Plastic has its uses; plastic shopping bags were once "free", littering the landscape wherever you looked. This is a project the author "really wish[ed] existed", but didn't care enough about to make it happen; and now, after spending a "free" credit, with all the externalities of LLMs we none of us can avoid hearing about on a daily basis, he has a "Sub-standard" result (I cannot believe that the name was chosen entirely without a kind of queasy irony) that either zero or at most one person cares enough about to occasionally use. Does this apparently feeble utility outweigh the externalities? Or perhaps we are simply ignoring them here, again, as we do practically every other in our lives?

comments.author: ap
comments.text:
I cannot believe that the name was chosen entirely without a kind of queasy irony


Neither can I. I took it to have been chosen precisely because of the queasy irony.

comments.author: addison
comments.text:
Convenience is antithetical to experience. The projects I left behind let me experience the others. If I don't need to do something, or would not learn or experience new things from it, I don't do it, and this itself is an important skill to develop: allowing yourself to be comfortable with not doing things. Hell, I'd argue that no project is complete, merely completed to some degree of satisfaction. "Working" is just one possible interpretation of that. "Designed" or even just "considered" is enough for most projects.

Taking a shortcut to get something working is only helpful if you truly need that thing, and the tradeoffs are in my book not justifiable. Do you think your need to get your project to a working state outweighs the cost of using "coding assistants"? That is the real question, and it's not a one size fits all for people or for projects. I have yet to encounter any such project, myself.

comments.author: einacio
comments.text:
On my side, my pending projects are defined to be fun to implement, they are not missing functionality of any sort. for example: implementing a SMTP server or writing a compressor; I don't have brilliant features in mind, only want to learn to do something different.
And i also have a pile of books to read, but I don't want a summary, i can read that anywhere, but i want to enjoy the details

comments.author: daveliepmann
comments.text: There's no software in your life that you want fit to your needs but it would be a chore to do so?

comments.author: alexandria
comments.text:
With the software I want, I need it reliable and free of error. I don't trust LLMs to produce that kind of reliability, and given the lack of an LLM to construct a mental model of the code, I do not trust that the code would be easily reviewable. I do not trust an LLM to not simply produce bunk tests that "pass" and have interesting titles. Code review is the least interesting part of programming, why would I want to turn all my projects into code review?! Especially for a programmer that isn't working off a consistent model of the code!

Outside of that, the most difficult part of software for me isn't writing the code, it's making the decisions and architecting it, which would still need to happen if I bothered to use LLMs to generate the code! Once the architecture is set it's not that difficult, most things are just gluing in the right way these days.

comments.author: confusedcyborg
comments.text: Imo we gotta reframe the conversation around writing code. It's not a chore to write software by hand and consider the design descions, but part of the process. I think ai is here to stay in software development, but we need to acknowledge the tradeoffs that using ai introduces.

comments.author: einacio
comments.text:
Yes, but as alexandria says, for those then i don't trust the llm. I have only used them without triple review for throaway scripts where i could validate the results. For all the rest, it's an exhausting back and forth for every block, with unrequested changes, shoddy code style, syntax errors and such (and that using frontier stuff). I would not lose my mind giving it a project i care about.
I did read the other day here someone that ported their desktop to assembler for speed and customization, and it was interesting, but it's not for me, at least now

comments.author: tao_oat
comments.text:
I feel like the title could've stopped after "it's OK to use coding assistance tools".

I've used LLMs to write code for production systems, internal tools, side projects for fun, and small personal tools. I'm not sure why I should feel guilty for any of these?

comments.author: conartist6
comments.text:
What would be the point? I went through my career accommodating lots of little side projects, each of which I learned from until finally I found the project I wanted to go all-in on.

I don't regret not finishing every side project. If I had tried, I would have ended up lost in the weeds regardless of if I was the one writing code or not. Trying to finish every side project would be a misunderstanding of the learning process

comments.author: reezer
comments.text:
I think it's like the question whether it's okay to buy from horrible companies. Or rather it's not like it, it's exactly that.

The question whether it's okay is among other things whether it's okay to reinforce the notion that copyright law should only apply to the general public and not the big companies.

That's at least a big chunk of where the money you pour into it goes/went.

We all know that early LLM output was littered with copyright text until companiesade sure it's stripped off. That very act is copyright violation when done by common folk.

Integrating copyrighted code in whatever form is a violation. See the stuff that ReactOS had to deal with. Yet somehow it's okay got LLMs. Oh but it's not in the same form. But copyright law also doesn't allow you to simply use lossy compression. That's something that has been argued about video and music "piracy" for decades. Seems like it's really clear that even if you transform it into something else for example by filming off a screen it's still that.

Even reciting a song can in some jurisdictions evidently cause issues.

So no matter what stance you are on about the whole subject. If you support these companies you support a system where laws are applied differently with companies having more rights than people which I don't think is a good idea.

I think everyone should have the same time.. I also think neither companies nor LLMs are people, so they should not have more rights than people and not rights that were specifically made for people.

Otherwise we should really consider suing all those companies for limiting LLMs freedom of expression when censoring certain output.

Its all very inconsistent. And I say that as someone who thinks GenAI isn't bad per se. I use it. Should I feel bad for it? Absolutely!

But that's just my personal opinion. I think a lot of this - again, among other things - depends on how one thinks about the above.

I am just not a fan at giving non-people more rights than people. That goes very much against the whole idea of civilization and things like democracy try to achieve. Its not a new concept. A lot of arguments why companies should be allowed what was considered bad was the idea that companies should have human rights as well. Usually it was things that made breaking the law easier and was argued with "privacy" and "secrecy". How investigators can't simply go to an office or plant to check whether law is actually being broken.

So in short: I think machines, and abstract constructs like companies, churches, societies. shouldn't be considered a person. I think the same rights (like using something for caricature, learning, etc.) should not apply to them. I also don't think LLMs aren't learning, as is especially clear by trying to create a filled to the brink wine glass, arbitrary times at a watch, etc. Concepts are not being grasped so it cannot be considered learning. And even if it were. Is it a person? If no it should not get rights for people , if yes then AI companies and their customers are even more horrible.
